memory_lessons.applicability: The prior one-stage CTA reduction is a useful measured comparator, but its complete-call timing does not isolate the weight-gradient kernel. The split variant needs its own correctness and complete-call measurements.
memory_lessons.claim: The one-stage CTA variant was valid and measured at 0.014375 s mean, compared with the valid baseline at 0.035464 s; neither measurement attributes time to this kernel alone.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Compare this tiled scratch reduction against the one-stage CTA result using the same complete-call harness.

proposal.hypothesis: The earlier valid one-CTA-per-(h,j) variant distributes B*L across threads but still leaves each output reduction within one CTA. For sufficiently large B*L, splitting into 65,536-element tiles creates multiple CTAs per output, writes one FP32 sum per tile to supplied scratch, then reduces those partials in a final CTA. The tile-count cap bounds the partial array to at most B*H*L floats; small reductions or unsupported tile counts use the direct CTA path. More parallel work may help large reductions, while the extra launch and scratch traffic may regress complete-call timing, so the controller must compare correctness and whole-call time.

retained: Replace the serial weight-gradient kernel with a direct CTA-level reduction for small or fallback cases.
For sufficiently large B*L, compute tiled FP32 partial sums in the supplied scratch buffer and finalize each (h,j) output in a second kernel.
Cap the tile count so the partial buffer contains at most B*H*L floats; every final-kernel partial read is preceded by a write in the same call.
